what: The register of UX failures and gaps. One entry per finding; every page, count, index and filter on this site is generated from this file. A failure is something that works against the reader; a gap is something the reader needs that is not there.

findings.title: The first phone screen explains how the site is built, not what it is about
findings.evidence: At 390×844 the first screen holds a two-row header, a "For agents /llms.txt" strip, three lines of metadata, a tagline about method, a second navigation bar and an editor's note. The lead story starts on screen two.
findings.impact: A contact who taps a link cannot tell in one screen that this is a publication about AI agents, security and publishing, or why they were sent it.
findings.fix: One sentence on what this is, who writes it, three doors (security, builders, news) and the lead, all on screen one. Everything else moves below or into the menu.

findings.title: The home page is 59 phone screens long, with 845 links
findings.evidence: The phone home page measures 49,715 px: Latest, Highlights, desk notes, collections, the full article list, then a map of every article's links.
findings.impact: The front page tries to show everything, so it chooses nothing for the reader. Nobody scrolls 59 screens; the curation is invisible.
findings.fix: Cut the home page to the lead, three per desk, collections and the newsletter. Lists and the link map move to their own pages.

findings.title: The masthead line describes a method, not a subject
findings.evidence: The tagline is "one page, one argument, with the figures, the data and the links to check it". Nothing says agents, AI governance, security or news economics.
findings.impact: The one line every visitor reads tells them how the site works instead of what it is about.
findings.fix: A masthead line that names the subject and the author, e.g. "Field notes on AI agents, security and the next generation of publishing, by Dinis Cruz".

findings.title: The edition label is older than the articles under it
findings.evidence: The home page says "Edition of 2026-10-08" above ten articles dated 10 October. Still the case in v0.7.1, above articles from 10 and 11 October.
findings.impact: A front page that looks three days stale on the day it was published tells a reader the site is not kept.
findings.fix: Date the edition from the newest article at build time, or label it as the editor's pick of its date.

findings.title: The version number is shown three times on the first screen
findings.evidence: v0.7.1 appears three times on the desktop first screen: in the agent strip, the metadata lines and the footer badge.
findings.impact: Engineering detail repeated where a reader looks first; it reads as a demo, not a publication.
findings.fix: One version, in the workshop and the page foot, linked to what changed. None on the reader's first screen.

findings.title: A "For agents /llms.txt" strip sits above the masthead
findings.evidence: The first element on every page is a strip addressed to agents, above the publication's name.
findings.impact: Useful to agents, noise to a person, and it takes the most valuable line on the screen.
findings.fix: Move it to the page head (link rel) and the footer, where agents look anyway. Satisfies both the Architect and the Designer on the panel.

findings.title: The editor's note is written for someone who read the last two editions
findings.evidence: The note opens "Third edition... the last two days", assuming the reader has followed along.
findings.impact: The one personal voice on the front page talks past the newcomer the page most needs to win.
findings.fix: Write the note for a newcomer: what this edition is about and where to start.

findings.title: Content is hidden until JavaScript runs
findings.evidence: The body starts at opacity 0 and only appears when a "ready" class is added, with a 1.6 s fallback.
findings.impact: On a slow phone, or for any reader or agent that does not run the script, the page is blank.
findings.fix: Render visible by default; animate only enhancements.

findings.title: Two navigation bars, and a 60-link menu that mixes reading with building
findings.evidence: A second bar of nine links repeats the menu. The menu holds about 60 links in nine groups (57 links in 8 groups when the lab mapped it), mixing reader pages (Newsletter, Collections) with builder pages (Replicate, Admin, Release history, The run log).
findings.impact: The reader has to sort the publication from the workshop themselves, twice.
findings.fix: One navigation. The publication on top; the workshop behind one item with its own front page.

findings.title: Missing pages show the default GitHub Pages 404
findings.evidence: Any missing URL shows GitHub's generic error page, with no link back to the newsroom.
findings.impact: A mistyped or old link ends the visit on a page that does not even say which site it is.
findings.fix: A branded 404.html with search and the three entry doors.

findings.title: Links without extensions in one article
findings.evidence: future-of-news links to /thesis, /portugal and /economics/rails, unlike every other link on the site.
findings.impact: They depend on the host resolving extensionless paths; on a strict host or a mirror they break.
findings.fix: Use the full .html or trailing-slash form everywhere; check it at build.

findings.title: Each article ends with seven next steps instead of one
findings.evidence: After the rating scales the foot of an article offers many routes onward with equal weight.
findings.impact: At the moment the reader is most ready to continue, the page makes them choose among seven.
findings.fix: One next step: the next part of the series, or the next "start here" piece for the reader's desk, then the newsletter.

findings.title: One topic holds more than half the articles
findings.evidence: "Agents & policy" holds 35 of 67 articles (38 of 73 in the lab's snapshot). The other five topics hold 13 to 26 and overlap: an article sits in about two.
findings.impact: A CISO who picks the obvious topic still faces 35 long reads. The classification does not help anyone choose.
findings.fix: Desks by audience, not internal topic: security, building, vaults, news, strategy (18 / 17 / 14 / 15 / 9 in the lab).

findings.title: Tags are not links, and there are no tag pages
findings.evidence: The lead article carries 12 tag pills; none links anywhere. Tags mix subjects, formats and product names ("article", "riskmandate"). 339 raw tags, 228 used once.
findings.impact: The most precise way into the archive looks clickable and goes nowhere.
findings.fix: A controlled vocabulary of about 40 tags owned by the Librarian, a page per tag, tags as links capped at five per article (339 → 42 in the lab; median 11 → 4).

findings.title: Filters cannot be shared
findings.evidence: Choosing a topic on the article list does not change the address.
findings.impact: You cannot send a contact "the security articles"; you can only send the whole list and an instruction.
findings.fix: Put every filter in the address (/articles/?desk=security, or in the path where query strings are not allowed).

findings.title: Series are invisible
findings.evidence: The reading meter in five pieces, the homepage diagnosis and its rebuild, the agent team in three depths: nothing says "part 2 of 5" or offers the next part. The lab found eleven series.
findings.impact: Readers land in the middle of a story without knowing there is a beginning.
findings.fix: Series pages with part numbers, previous / next on each part, and the reader's progress.

findings.title: There is no "start here" path
findings.evidence: The Historian's weekly note and the collections are the best orientation on the site, and they sit below the fold.
findings.impact: A newcomer facing 73 long articles has no way to know which five to read first.
findings.fix: Each desk opens with "Start here: five articles in order", written by the Historian.

findings.title: Cards do not show reading time or format
findings.evidence: The median article is about 4,500 words and 25 of 66 are over 5,000, yet no card shows reading time or whether it is a field report, explainer, analysis or desk note.
findings.impact: A reader with three minutes cannot tell a note from a 40-minute analysis before opening it.
findings.fix: Reading time and a format label on every card, derived at build.

findings.title: Search only matches titles, teasers and tags
findings.evidence: The search box does not look inside articles, although a markdown twin of every article exists.
findings.impact: About 300,000 words are unsearchable; a reader who remembers a phrase cannot find the piece.
findings.fix: Search over bodies and abstracts from the markdown twins, with snippets.

findings.title: The best reader feature is buried under metadata and a long italic abstract
findings.evidence: On the lead article (about 8,000 words) a phone reader scrolls past a three-line breadcrumb, a byline with two version numbers, 12 tag pills and a 250-word italic abstract before reaching the "Five readers" block.
findings.impact: The short version that would let a reader decide is found only by those who already decided to read.
findings.fix: Title and standfirst; a byline that says how it was made, date and reading time; the short version in three or four sentences; reader views as one row; then the article. Tags and versions to the foot.

findings.title: Author tooling is shown to every reader
findings.evidence: Every article ends with "Posting this article on LinkedIn?" and the cover image's filename.
findings.impact: A tool for the author, printed on every reader's copy.
findings.fix: Move it to an admin view, or behind an author flag.

findings.title: The byline names one human; the AI authorship is in the footer
findings.evidence: Articles are written from voice notes by a desk of named agents; the byline says only "Dinis Cruz" and the agent newsroom is credited in the footer.
findings.impact: A reader who finds the disclosure late reads it as something hidden, on a publication whose pitch is provenance.
findings.fix: "Dinis Cruz, written with the SGit agent newsroom" in the byline, linked to the purpose page.

findings.title: There is no page that says why the publication exists
findings.evidence: The agenda (build sgit.ai and RiskMandate, which most articles use as evidence), the licences and the participant disclosure are spread across the footer and method pages.
findings.impact: Readers cannot judge the argument without knowing who is making it and why.
findings.fix: A purpose page, linked from the masthead and every byline: the agenda, open by default, how it is written, who it is for, what I want from you.

findings.title: All three rating scales start on 3
findings.evidence: The usefulness, more-like-this and level-of-detail scales at the foot of every article are preselected on the middle value.
findings.impact: Neither the reader nor the author can tell "not rated" from "useful". Every rating collected so far is ambiguous.
findings.fix: Start unselected; record only real taps.

findings.title: Ratings never reach the author
findings.evidence: Ratings stay in the reader's browser unless they choose to send their whole reading record.
findings.impact: The first contacts sent to the site teach the author nothing about what landed.
findings.fix: One-tap send by default, with plain consent ("Send this rating to Dinis, anonymous"), through the encrypted append lane, with a local receipt.

findings.title: There is no way to say what was missing
findings.evidence: Feedback is three scales and nothing else: no free text, no "write about this", no "I need a new version".
findings.impact: Scores say what, not why. Requests that would become the next pitches have no channel.
findings.fix: One optional line ("What would have made this more useful?") and request buttons, sent through the append lane with a receipt.

findings.title: Articles join the reader's list without being asked
findings.evidence: Opening an article adds it to the reader's reading list automatically.
findings.impact: The list stops meaning "what I chose to keep" and becomes a history the reader did not ask for.
findings.fix: Make "Keep" a tap.

findings.title: The £5.00 balance chip has no label
findings.evidence: An unlabelled "£5.00" sits in the header of every page. Still unlabelled in v0.7.1.
findings.impact: An amount of money with no explanation reads as a bill or a trap; the synthetic-user study flagged it.
findings.fix: Label it "£5 free reading credit".

findings.title: Opening an article charges a penny with no notice
findings.evidence: The chip changes from £5.00 to £4.99 on opening any article, silently. In the synthetic-user study this exact moment made a retired reader ask whether she owed money.
findings.impact: The first thing a new reader learns about the reading meter is that their balance dropped without being told.
findings.fix: Announce the first charge once, in words, at the moment it happens.

findings.title: "Credit can go below zero" reads as a debt
findings.evidence: The account page says credit can go below zero.
findings.impact: Readers hear "you can owe us money", on a site that has not asked them for any.
findings.fix: Say what actually happens when the free credit is used up, in reader terms.

findings.title: "You pay the price" reads as a warning
findings.evidence: The caption under the usefulness scale reads "You pay the price".
findings.impact: The feature (your rating sets what the page costs you) is a benefit; the wording makes it a threat.
findings.fix: "Your rating sets what this page costs you".

findings.title: Nothing shows real money moving
findings.evidence: No counts of readers, payments or revenue anywhere. A blocking finding of the synthetic-user study, still open.
findings.impact: Readers and publishers asking "is this a real business?" find no answer.
findings.fix: Public reader numbers (ratings, readers, payments), generated and dated.

findings.title: It is unclear how a writer gets paid
findings.evidence: The site states nothing is paid upstream yet, and does not say what will be. A blocking finding of the synthetic-user study.
findings.impact: Writers and publishers, the people the meter is pitched to, cannot see where their share comes from.
findings.fix: Say plainly what is paid today (nothing), what is planned and when.

findings.title: No contact for a pilot on the Replicate page
findings.evidence: The page that invites publishers to replicate the newsroom has no name, email or form.
findings.impact: The one reader ready to act has nowhere to go. A blocking finding of the synthetic-user study.
findings.fix: A name and email for pilots on Replicate and on the account pages; move the publishers page to the newsroom with the same contact.

findings.title: The top-up page said "simulated" while asking for money
findings.evidence: The synthetic-user run of 10 October found the top-up page asking for a payment while describing itself as simulated.
findings.impact: A payment page that says it is not real is a payment page nobody can trust.
findings.fix: Describe the one real Stripe payment. Done in v0.6.4; real Stripe top-up live since 11 October.
findings.status_note: Fixed by v0.6.4: the page now describes one Stripe payment.

findings.title: Articles were published on two domains, and diverged
findings.evidence: sgit.ai/articles/ served five 11 October articles (e.g. no-server-by-design, the-agent-is-the-reader) that returned 404 on newsroom.sgit.ai.
findings.impact: The same publication was more complete on the wrong site.
findings.fix: Publish once to the newsroom; make sgit.ai link or redirect there.
findings.status_note: Fixed in v0.7.1: all six 11 October articles are live on the newsroom; the count is 73.

findings.title: Two domains claim to be canonical for the same article
findings.evidence: sgit.ai/articles/hope-or-enforcement.html declares canonical sgit.ai; the newsroom copy declares canonical newsroom.sgit.ai.
findings.impact: Search engines split the article's standing between two copies, and readers can land on either.
findings.fix: One canonical, the newsroom; a 301 or a canonical pointing there from sgit.ai.

findings.title: Three different article counts
findings.evidence: sgit.ai said 72, the newsroom home said 67, llms.txt said 66, on the same day.
findings.impact: When a site cannot count itself, the reader doubts every other number on it.
findings.fix: Generate every count from one manifest at build, and fail the release if any page disagrees.
findings.status_note: wire.json says 73 in v0.7.1; the three surfaces were not re-compared.

findings.title: The feed is titled for the old site
findings.evidence: articles/feed.xml is titled "sgit.ai articles".
findings.impact: Subscribers see the wrong publication name in their reader.
findings.fix: Retitle it "SGit Newsroom", from the same source as the masthead.

findings.title: The study page reports a fixed bug as current
findings.evidence: The synthetic-user page says 51 vault images 404; all images now load (0 broken across 10 articles).
findings.impact: A visitor reading the study believes the site is broken in a way it no longer is.
findings.fix: A dated "fixed in v0.6.x" note beside the finding.

findings.title: 51 vault images missing across 10 articles
findings.evidence: The third synthetic-user run found 51 vault images returning 404 in 10 articles.
findings.impact: Evidence images are the point of an evidence-first article; broken ones undo the claim.
findings.fix: Fixed: 0 broken images on 10 rendered articles in v0.6.4.

findings.title: Persona links were designed but not live
findings.evidence: Persona links (/for/ciso and others) were described in articles but no URL existed to send a contact.
findings.impact: Every contact got the same front page, made for nobody in particular.
findings.fix: Ship persona links for the main audiences.
findings.status_note: Fixed in v0.7.1: /persona/founder/ and four others, an index page, copyable links and links.json for agents.

findings.title: Opening a persona link adds it to the browser without asking
findings.evidence: Opening a persona page silently adds the persona to the reader's browser.
findings.impact: The reader did not choose to become "a founder" on this site; it was done to them.
findings.fix: Show the persona and offer "Read as" and "Keep" as separate choices.

findings.title: The founder page says "the picks above" and no picks render on a phone
findings.evidence: On a phone with no prior visit, the founder persona page refers to picks that are not shown.
findings.impact: The page a founder is sent to points at content that is not there, on the first visit, which is the only one that matters.
findings.fix: Render the picks on the landing view with no prior state; test it in a fresh browser.

findings.title: Persona pages are a list, with no story, opinion or next step
findings.evidence: Each persona page is seven starting articles plus an explanation of how the link works.
findings.impact: A persona link is a promise that the site was made for this reader; a list does not keep it.
findings.fix: One front-page template filled from a persona file: masthead, story, Dinis's note, start here, sections, board, "what is missing?", other readers.

findings.title: Setting location.hash inside a vault app re-navigates the frame: every link silently dead
findings.where: any vault app that routes by hash
findings.evidence: In the host the app is an about:srcdoc frame, where assigning location.hash re-navigates instead of firing hashchange. The How Much Evidence vault shipped on 5 October 2026 with every view link dead.
findings.impact: An app that works when opened as a file ships to readers with no working navigation, and nothing errors.
findings.fix: Keep the route in a variable; catch a[href^="#"] in a capture click handler; mark links data-sg-native; use the hash only when running standalone. Documented in the sgit.ai guidance.

source.label: Design lab: what building it measured

findings.status_note: Open as a platform trap; every lab vault avoids it.

findings.title: localStorage throws inside the vault app frame, so reader data is lost on reload
findings.where: any vault app that stores reader state
findings.evidence: The app frame refuses localStorage with SecurityError. Lab kit v0.1.2 kept highlights, notes and ratings only until reload.
findings.impact: A reader's notes disappear on reload, the worst failure a note-taking feature can have.
findings.fix: Store through the host's async sg.state (survives reload). Kit v0.1.3 does; every lab vault was republished on it.

source.label: Design lab: what building it measured

findings.status_note: Open as a platform trap; fixed in the lab by kit v0.1.3.

findings.title: A vault app can load images and scripts from a site but cannot fetch its data
findings.evidence: The host CSP is connect-src blob: data:. fetch() to newsroom.sgit.ai is refused although it sends access-control-allow-origin *, while and classic
findings.impact: Builders reasonably expect CORS-open data to be readable and discover otherwise in production; apps must snapshot data instead.
findings.fix: Snapshot the data into the vault (with SHA-256 in sources.json) and say in the UI which copy is shown. State the CSP where builders read about vault apps.

source.label: Design lab: what building it measured

findings.title: Query strings break inside the vault host, so filters must live in the route path
findings.evidence: Adding a query string to an app route breaks in the srcdoc frame.
findings.impact: The usual way to make a filter linkable is not available; each app has to invent a path encoding.
findings.fix: Encode filters in the path in a fixed order (desk, format, tag, series, month, q), as the findability vault does.

source.label: Design lab: what building it measured

findings.title: File-path pills scrolled the whole page sideways at 390 px
findings.where: lab kit v0.1.1, all prototype vaults
findings.evidence: Long, unbreakable file-path pills on the data pages pushed the page wider than a phone.
findings.impact: Sideways scroll on a phone makes every line harder to read and hides the edge of the content.
findings.fix: Let pills wrap; the gate now fails on any sideways scroll at 390 px. Fixed in kit v0.1.2.

source.label: Design lab: what building it measured

findings.title: Re-rendering the whole view on every save lost the reader's place
findings.evidence: Every store write (a highlight, a note, a status) re-rendered the whole reading view and jumped the scroll position.
findings.impact: A reader who highlights a sentence is thrown somewhere else in an 8,000-word article.
findings.fix: Repaint only the parts that changed. Done in the article vault before publishing.

source.label: Design lab: what building it measured

findings.title: A highlight across paragraphs is cut at the first paragraph
findings.evidence: Selecting text that spans two paragraphs and tapping Highlight keeps only the part in the first.
findings.impact: The reader loses part of what they chose to keep, without being told.
findings.fix: Store highlights as ranges across blocks, or refuse the selection with a message.

source.label: Design lab: what building it measured

findings.title: Search results show no snippets
findings.evidence: The findability prototype searches a 98 KB term index; results are cards with no matching text.
findings.impact: A reader cannot see why a result matched, so cannot judge it before opening.
findings.fix: Snippets from the markdown twins, within a size budget, or computed on a site page rather than in the vault.

source.label: Design lab: what building it measured

findings.title: Stacked tables on a phone lose their column labels
findings.evidence: At 390 px the prototype stacks table rows into blocks without repeating the column names.
findings.impact: Values without labels on a phone: the reader has to remember what each line means.
findings.fix: Repeat the column label in each stacked cell (data-label + ::before).

source.label: Design lab: what building it measured

findings.title: "Ask the article" has never run against a real on-device model
findings.evidence: The ask view uses Chrome's built-in model when present and a labelled extractive fallback otherwise. Only the fallback and a stub were tested; the model is absent in headless Chrome and likely in the vault frame.
findings.impact: The feature is shown to readers on a path nobody has seen work.
findings.fix: Test in a real Chrome with the model, or use sg.llm with an llm.chat grant; until then say "fallback" in the UI, as it does.

source.label: Design lab: what building it measured

findings.title: Scrolling back up a little puts focus in the address bar and opens the keyboard
findings.environment: Firefox for iOS on an iPad, landscape, reading newsroom.sgit.ai/admin/versions.html (newsroom v0.12.120)
findings.evidence: Reading a long page, a small scroll back up brings the hidden toolbars back, the address field gets focus with its URL selected, and the on-screen keyboard opens over the bottom half of the page (second screenshot: the URL selected, Cancel showing, the keyboard covering the release table). Nothing on the page was tapped on purpose. A likely mechanism, not yet confirmed: the toolbar slides in under the finger mid-gesture, so the touch that was a scroll lands on the address field as a tap.
findings.impact: The reader was not asking to go anywhere, and loses half the screen to a keyboard. Worse, it looks like the page has a bug: the first reading was that the site had somehow started an edit. The browser's fault is charged to the site, and the reader's concentration is broken either way.
findings.fix: For the browser: a scroll gesture never focuses the address field; only a deliberate tap on a toolbar that is already at rest does. For the sites: nothing a page can prevent, but worth knowing that readers will report it as our bug, so it is recorded here with its real owner.

source.label: Reported by Dinis Cruz, 18 Oct 2026, with screenshots

images.alt: Firefox on iPad after a small scroll up: the tab strip and address bar are back, the URL is selected for editing and the keyboard covers the lower half of the newsroom release history
images.caption: After a small scroll up: address field focused, URL selected, keyboard open. Nothing on the page was tapped.

findings.title: The toolbars come back on any small scroll up, taking screen and moving the page
findings.environment: Firefox for iOS on an iPad, landscape, reading newsroom.sgit.ai/admin/versions.html (newsroom v0.12.120)
findings.evidence: Scrolled down, Firefox shows only a thin address line and the page gets almost the whole screen (first screenshot: the newsroom header starts about 90 px down a 1,640 px screen). Any small scroll up restores the tab strip and full address bar (second screenshot: the header starts about 270 px down), about 180 px or 11% of the screen, and the page content shifts down by that much while it is being read. The hidden state is the one wanted all the time.
findings.impact: The reader scrolls up a line to re-read a sentence and the whole page jumps, the text moves away from their eyes, and a toolbar they did not ask for takes a ninth of the screen. Each time, attention goes to the chrome instead of the text.
findings.fix: For the browser: keep the toolbars hidden until a deliberate gesture (a tap on the address line, or a scroll to the very top), and offer a setting to keep them collapsed. For the sites, on our side of the line: keep our own sticky header as small as it can be, because it stacks on top of the browser's (on this page the newsroom's header takes about another 110 px).

source.label: Reported by Dinis Cruz, 18 Oct 2026, with screenshots

images.alt: Firefox on iPad scrolled down: only a thin address line above the newsroom header, the release history filling the screen
images.caption: Scrolled down: toolbars collapsed to a thin address line. This is the state wanted all the time.

images.alt: The same page after a small scroll up, with the tab strip and address bar back
images.caption: After a small scroll up: tab strip and address bar back, the page pushed down about 180 px (and, here, the keyboard too: UX-056).
